lectures.title: Managing Storage with Partition Tables: MBR vs GPT

cues.en: Let's now have a look at the structure of a storage device.
Please note in this lecture I'm mostly referring to hard disk drives, SSDs or USB drives.
I'm excluding, for example, optical disk or other storage devices from this lecture.
So other storage devices might, for example, be tape storage, cloud storage and so on because they
may work slightly differently, um, or in case of cloud storage completely differently.
So here I'm mostly referring to hard disks, SSDs and USB drives or SD cards or something like this.
So let's have a look at the structure of such a storage device.
The way it works that we can store many bits on that device in a consecutive order and we want to be
able to define how we want to store the data there.
And for that we are able to create a so-called partition table.
The partition table is responsible for managing or for dividing that device into areas where we can
store our data.
Just to give you an example.
Let's say, for example, we have two operating systems on our computer, maybe a dual boot between
with a Linux and a Windows machine.
Both of them want to have their own area where they can just store their data.
So we could create a partition.
And one partition of that device would be for the Linux part and the other partition would be for the
Windows part of the computer, and then we could just reboot the computer and then it would boot up
properly.
So in order to create this structure and we create that structure, even if we only have one partition
on our computer, we need a partition table.
And there are two formats there.
The one is MBR, that's the so-called master boot record.
That's the older partitioning scheme.
It's limited to four primary partitions and it's limited to about two terabytes of disk size.
So nowadays we don't really use it that much anymore.
We mostly use the GPT, the Guid partition table.
That's a more modern partitioning scheme.
It supports up to 128 partitions.
So imagine we could have like 100, almost 128 operating systems we could choose from on one drive and
each of those could have their own partition.
So you can imagine that's pretty much enough usually.
And we also support larger disks.
So that's that would be the way to go.
We can visualize those partitions with tools like Gparted.
So let's have a look at how we can visualize that with a user interface.
Later, we will also have a look at how we can visualize or at least see it on the command line so I
can start the program.
